Tobin was at the pump house when she came up the path, doing something to the valve with a wrench that was wrong for the job.

"That's the wrong wrench," Maren said.

"It's the wrench I have." He didn't look up. Water seeped from the fitting in a thin bright thread and ran down the pipe and disappeared into the boards. "Your line's been knocking all week. Alba can hear it from her porch."

"Alba can hear a moth land in the next county."

"She can," he said, "and also your line's been knocking." He got the jaw seated and leaned on it. The fitting gave with a sound like a knuckle. The seep quit. "There. Tell me that's not better."

"It's better." She set the bucket down on the step. "You want coffee for that, or money?"

"I want the coffee and I want to borrow your ladder."

"The ladder's got a cracked rung."

"I know," he said. "I cracked it."

She looked at him. He wiped the wrench on his thigh and looked back, easy, the way he'd looked at her across desks and fences and one hospital bed for forty years.

"Third rung," she said finally. "Step over it."

"I always do."

She put the coffee on and he sat on the step with the wrench across his knee like a cat that might leave. Steam climbed off the kettle; the window went gray with it. Out on the flats the tide was coming back in, and the knocking in the line was gone, and the morning had the shape of most of their mornings, which she supposed was the point of him.

"Clams for chowder," he said, tilting his head at the bucket. "You'll want cream."

"I have cream."

"You had cream in June."

"Go home, Tobin," she said, and poured his cup first.
